Fourier-Laplace slices and boundary poles

Original edition by GPT-6.1 Sol (OpenAI), Ultra reasoning effort. Repaired and self-checked by GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), Ultra reasoning effort, October 2026. Original exposition: public domain (CC0); supplied prerequisites retain their stated licences.

Suppose an analytic function is observed along several horizontal lines. What information do those observations contain about its inverse Fourier transform? A pointwise formula may hide a removable pole; an entire continuation may coexist with input on both sides of the origin. The useful data are the square-integral norms of the slices, together with their dependence on height.

We first calculate these data for a pulse of finite duration and for a Gaussian. The calculations distinguish support information from analytic continuation and show why the sign of the Fourier kernel matters. A common inverse-transform lemma then makes this interpretation rigorous for arbitrary square-integrable slices. The half-plane theorem recovers a one-sided input; the strip theorem recovers two exponential tail bounds. The common input determines a convex domain of finite slice norms; its logarithmic curvature is a covariance matrix, and its large-height slopes recover the actual compact support hull. Finally, adding two boundary traces becomes an inverse problem for a nonvanishing frequency multiplier.

We use , inverse factor , , and complex bilinear distributional pairings.

The supplied Fourier foundation, F1–F5, proves every Schwartz transform, Gaussian integral, inverse and transpose rule used here. Separated frequencies and distributional order, Lemma0.1, proves Schwartz Plancherel. The supplied integration foundation, §§15.0–15.4 and16, proves measure, convergence, product integration, linear Jacobians, the norm inequalities, completeness and compact smooth density. The scalar foundation, §§12–13, and finite algebra, §§10.1–10.6, supply the elementary calculus and matrix operations. We give the required completed square-integral Fourier maps below and prove the slice estimates with scalar Cauchy–Schwarz and Tonelli.

The exact Cauchy and Taylor formulas, finite-regularity boundary theorem and pole jumps are Cauchy kernels and distributional boundary limits, Theorem1.1, Corollary2.2, Theorem3.1, Corollary3.2 and Theorem4.1. The several-variable power-series construction and connected identity principle are Holomorphic boundaries in convex cones, Section3 and Lemma3.1.

Completing the square-integral Fourier maps

Lemma 0.1. The Schwartz Fourier transform and its inverse extend uniquely to mutually inverse continuous maps on , with They agree with the tempered-distribution transforms and, on , with the ordinary integral transform.

Proof. By integration §15.3, choose tending to in . U041, Lemma0.1, gives Completeness therefore defines . The same equality proves independence of the approximating sequence, linearity, the exact norm and uniqueness of a continuous extension. Since on Schwartz functions and reflection is an isometry, the same construction gives the stated inverse norm. The two compositions equal the identity on the dense Schwartz subspace by F4; continuity extends both identities to all of . This proves surjectivity as well as injectivity.

Every function defines a tempered distribution by Cauchy–Schwarz against a Schwartz test. For , scalar Fubini on the approximants gives Both sides pass to their limits by Cauchy–Schwarz. This is precisely the bilinear transpose definition in F5, so the completed and distributional transforms agree, with every differentiation and reflection sign retained. The inverse is treated identically. For , F5 also proves equality of the ordinary integral transform with that same distributional transform, by absolute Fubini. Its continuous integral representative consequently represents the completed transform almost everywhere.

Here and below, equality of locally functions as distributions gives equality almost everywhere. To see this directly, multiply their difference by any compact smooth cutoff . Then and pairs to zero with every Schwartz function, since is a compact test. Approximate in by compact smooth functions and pass the zero pairings by Cauchy–Schwarz; this gives . Cutoffs equal to one on an exhausting sequence of compact balls give almost everywhere. The same argument inside an open set uses compactly supported cutoffs there. This proves the local support identification used later.

Read the data before choosing a theorem

For a Fourier–Laplace transform with kernel , the height contributes , not . Thus positive heights emphasize the right tail and negative heights emphasize the left tail. With the Plancherel normalization already stated, the measured quantity is

Worked case: a pulse whose apparent pole disappears. Take . This pulse begins before zero and ends after zero. Direct integration over that finite interval gives

The integral expression is entire: on every compact set of , every complex derivative is dominated by an integrable function on . The quotient seems to have a pole at , but the numerator vanishes there as well. Its value is , obtained from the integral, so the singularity is removable.

The weighted input gives a more informative measurement:

This is finite at every height, including the one at which the quotient in (R2) looks singular. Its large-height behavior records both endpoints:

Indeed, as , ; as , the numerator tends to one in (R3). Taking logarithms gives (R4), because the logarithm of the denominator divided by tends to zero. In particular is unbounded as . The pulse has an entire transform, yet fails the uniform lower-half-plane norm condition. Its negative-time part is exactly what that condition detects.

Worked case: an entire transform with two infinite tails. For , the Gaussian transform from the linked Fourier proof is . The real transform formula extends to every complex : the input integral is holomorphic by compact-height Gaussian domination, and the connected identity principle gives the extension. Completing the real square yields

The Gaussian mass is proved in the supplied Fourier foundation, F3. Every slice is square integrable, but neither half-plane has a uniform norm bound. Unlike (R4), the quotient has no finite endpoint limit: it tends to for positive heights and to for negative heights. This calculation is consistent with the input being nonzero arbitrarily far in both directions. Entire continuation, finite norms at each height, and uniformly bounded norms on a half-plane are three different pieces of information.

A local interpretation of the norm profile. For any nonzero compactly supported input, normalize the weighted square to a probability measure:

All height derivatives may pass under the integral because the support is compact. Thus and ; differentiating gives the two identities. Equality in the last line would concentrate at one point. This is impossible for a nonzero density with respect to Lebesgue measure. The slope is twice the weighted mean position, and the curvature is four times its variance. A height change is therefore a controlled change in what part of the input is emphasized. Exercise 4 proves the corresponding strict log-convex inequality for the broader strip class, without assuming compact support.

For data with only a local bound on the slice norms, the next lemma reconstructs one input compatible with all heights. A uniform bound across an entire lower half-plane has the additional force needed to exclude negative support. For a finite strip, the useful question instead concerns both endpoint weights.

L. A common inverse transform on horizontal slices

Lemma L. Let be nonempty, open and connected. Let be holomorphic on . Write . Suppose

There is one locally square-integrable function , independent of , such that

The transform in the first equality is the completed transform. Each weighted function in (L2) belongs to . No trace at the edge of is assumed.

Proof. Cauchy's coordinate-circle formula bounds the horizontal norm of every derivative uniformly on smaller compact sets of heights. Indeed choose a common coordinate radius whose imaginary-coordinate shifts stay in a compact subset of . The derivative formula is an integral of translates , in the differentiated coordinates, multiplied by factors of modulus at most . Real translations preserve the original norm. For clarity, no vector-valued integration theorem is required for this estimate. Parametrize the coordinate circles by their angles with normalized product measure . The Cauchy formula writes the derivative as , where is the modulus of the translated above. The scalar integral exists for every by continuity on the compact circle product. Cauchy–Schwarz in the probability measure and then Tonelli give The integrand is jointly continuous and hence measurable; (L1) bounds its integral. Real translation invariance now gives

The circle formulas follow from U013, Corollary2.2, one coordinate at a time, or from the full polydisk proof in U015, Section3. Choose the radius small enough that every simultaneous coordinate shift stays in the enlarged compact height set. The pointwise fundamental theorem along a height segment, followed by the same scalar integral inequality on the unit interval, gives Thus every derivative is locally Lipschitz in . Apply the fundamental theorem twice to its scalar values. The remainder after its first height derivative is an integral against , whose total mass is . Cauchy–Schwarz for this normalized nonnegative weight and Tonelli give Formula(L3) bounds the right side on each small height neighborhood. Division by proves norm differentiability with the stated derivative. Applying this in every coordinate and order, and telescoping along coordinate segments, proves smooth dependence. Its Cauchy–Riemann equation is .

Put . Lemma0.1 supplies the continuous completed inverse and its exact transpose agreement. It preserves the proved smooth dependence, and its distributional differentiation identity gives

The sign is fixed by . On a compact set of , multiplication by is a smooth distribution multiplier. Equation (L4) makes every height derivative of zero. For each compact smooth spatial test, its scalar pairing is smooth in height with every first derivative zero. Integrating along segments inside a ball shows that the pairing is locally constant. Its level set at a fixed height and its complement are both open, so connectedness makes the pairing constant throughout the height domain. This holds for every compact test; thus the distribution is independent of height. Fixing therefore gives the locally representative , and at every height. The original completed Plancherel identity gives (L2). This also proves uniqueness.

We will need (L1) when initially only an averaged entire norm is known. If is entire and is continuous, then

implies (L1) on every compact set of heights. For one complex variable, the Cauchy Taylor series and angular orthogonality give the disk mean inequality . To see the inequality without an unstated subharmonic theorem, on every smaller circle the mean square of is ; uniform convergence justifies the finite-series limit, and integration against gives the disk formula. Apply it successively in all coordinates. Integrating the resulting inequality over , enlarging the polydisk to a coordinate box, and translating its real coordinates gives

Tonelli applies even before finiteness of a slice is established. On a compact set of , the continuous positive weight has a positive minimum on its enlarged compact set. Thus the right side is uniformly bounded by a constant times (L5). Every slice, including any initially exceptional slice, is in ; the first part of the lemma now applies.

The heights with finite norms form a convex domain

Connectedness in Lemma L ties the slices to one input. That input itself determines a larger set of heights and a holomorphic extension.

Theorem L.1 (the finite-moment tube). For the input in Lemma L, put The set is convex, contains the original height domain, and contains its open convex hull. For and nonnegative weights summing to one, with zero weights omitted. The function extends to by the absolutely convergent integral All complex derivatives may be taken under that integral. In particular, the holomorphic extension to the tube over the convex hull of the original heights is unique.

Proof. If , and the extension is zero. Otherwise at every finite height. For positive weights in (T2), define the probability densities . Weighted arithmetic-geometric mean gives . To verify it, when and all factors are positive, sum with weights , then exponentiate. A zero factor makes the inequality immediate, as does . Integrating and restoring the norm factors gives (T2). Thus is convex.

Lemma L gives finiteness at every original height. Every point of its convex hull is a finite convex combination; one coefficient is positive, and moving its corresponding height inside a small ball in the original open set moves the combination through a ball. Hence this convex hull is open and lies in .

Fix , and choose so that every vertex , , lies in . If , then in the orthant , For every integer , Cauchy–Schwarz bounds the integral of times the right side by The latter integral is finite: bound by a finite sum of coordinate monomials and use repeated one-dimensional polynomial-exponential integrals. There are finitely many orthants. These bounds supply a single integrable majorant on the height neighborhood for each derivative order. Thus (T3) defines a holomorphic function, and At each original height the weighted input belongs both to and . The ordinary and completed Fourier transforms therefore coincide. Their continuous representatives agree everywhere, so the extension equals the given . Completed Plancherel proves the exact norm in (T3) at every interior height. The interior of a convex set is convex, and the connected identity principle gives uniqueness on this tube, and hence on the convex hull tube.

The interior of is the domain furnished by finite slice norms. It need not be the largest domain to which the holomorphic function can be continued. Nor does convex extension add a hard support condition to the input.

Curvature and the actual support function

The one-dimensional compact calculation (R6) holds on the whole interior finite-moment domain, with a full covariance matrix.

Theorem L.2 (moments and support from slice norms). Let be locally square integrable on , with as in (T1) and . At every interior height define All moments exist there, is smooth, and The Hessian is positive definite; is strictly convex on . If is compactly supported and is its actual closed convex support hull, then for any fixed ,

Proof. Use the same vertices as in (T4). On their orthants, for , The last polynomial-exponential factor is bounded: each nonnegative coordinate power times has finite maximum by elementary differentiation, and a finite monomial bound handles . The vertex density is integrable, and the finite sum over orthants gives an integrable majorant. Every height derivative passes under , and all moments are finite. In particular, Dividing and differentiating gives (T8). For nonzero real , the Hessian quadratic form is . If it were zero, the probability density would be concentrated on the affine hyperplane . Choose a coordinate with nonzero coefficient in ; each slice in that coordinate contains at most one point. Tonelli therefore makes this hyperplane a Lebesgue null set, contradicting the absolutely continuous probability mass. The Hessian is positive definite. Restriction to each nonconstant segment inside the convex interior gives a strictly positive second derivative, proving strict convexity.

For compact , all heights lie in . Put , a finite number. The positive base-height weight does not change null sets. For each , the set has positive weighted mass . Thus, for , Taking logarithms and dividing by , then taking and , proves that the limit is , including .

For locally inputs, vanishing as a distribution on an open set is equivalent to vanishing almost everywhere there. Hence its distributional support equals the support of . This measure is carried by the closed support: its complement is a countable union of basic open sets on which the measure is zero. A support point with would have a sufficiently small positive-mass neighborhood in that strict region, contradicting essential supremum. Conversely the supremum on the support bounds the essential supremum. Therefore is precisely the supremum on the actual support, which equals the supremum on its closed convex hull. This is , proving (T9).

Replacing by recovers the lower directional endpoint as . In one dimension this proves the endpoint rule in (R4) for every nonzero compact input, even when it vanishes on part of a larger containing interval. The factors and in (T8) come from the weight .

For the standard statistical interpretation of these derivatives, see Charles J. Geyer's Exponential Families, Sections 3.5–3.6 and 4. Its natural parameter is for the weighted density here. The domination and support arguments needed for the present Fourier–Laplace setting have been proved above.

A. The lower half-plane and the recovered boundary

Theorem A. For , extended by zero to the negative half-line,

is holomorphic and satisfies

Conversely every holomorphic lower-half-plane with finite supremum in (A2) is represented uniquely by (A1). Its horizontal boundary is recovered strongly in : as .

Proof. If , Cauchy–Schwarz makes (A1) absolutely integrable: . On any compact subset of the lower half-plane, every derivative is dominated by for a fixed ; its integral is finite by the same inequality. Differentiation under the integral proves holomorphy. At each height is the ordinary and completed transform of , so Plancherel gives . Monotone convergence as gives (A2), including the supremum. Dominated convergence gives in , hence the stated strong boundary.

For the converse write the finite supremum as . Lemma L yields a common locally with for every . Along , Fatou forces almost everywhere on : the integrand tends to infinity at every such point where . Along , Fatou then gives . The forward construction for this has the same completed transform on every slice. Both representatives are continuous in the real coordinate; equality almost everywhere on that slice is therefore equality everywhere. This proves the whole representation, the exact norm and the recovered trace without assuming any boundary value in advance.

The pulse calculation explains the converse: a fixed negative point is amplified without bound as the height tends to minus infinity. Fatou's lemma turns that observation into an almost-everywhere support statement even when no pointwise boundary function was given. Delaying a one-sided input changes the norm by an exponential factor; Exercise 2 derives that modified condition with either sign of delay.

B. Two weighted endpoints of a finite strip

Theorem B. Let be finite real numbers. If , , its Fourier–Laplace integral is holomorphic in and

Every holomorphic function in that strip with finite left side has one such representation. At either endpoint its slices converge strongly to the completed transform of .

Proof. On , write ; on , use . Cauchy–Schwarz on these half-lines proves absolute integrability of the Fourier–Laplace kernel and all its derivatives, uniformly on compact substrips. It also proves holomorphy by differentiation under the integral. Put . For , , scalar convexity of the real exponential gives

The integrable majorant gives at either endpoint. It also dominates up to a fixed factor, giving strong weighted convergence. Plancherel proves (B1) and both trace statements.

Conversely, if the left side is , Lemma L constructs with throughout the strip. Taking sequences of heights to either endpoint and using Fatou gives . The forward integral is therefore defined. Its completed slice transforms equal those of the given function by Lemma L, hence their continuous real-coordinate representatives agree everywhere. The forward proof now gives the exact equality and the endpoint traces.

The finite strip controls exponential tails rather than a hard support cutoff. Its norm need not be largest at the midpoint or have equal endpoint values. Theorem B gives the exact endpoint maximum; the two-tail input in Exercise 3 makes the asymmetry explicit. We now use the same height dependence in a different direction: the input will be determined by an equation relating two boundary observations.

C. A strip function with two boundary poles

Theorem C. There is exactly one holomorphic on for which is bounded on the whole strip and whose distributional traces satisfy

It is

Proof. First consider any function with the boundedness condition. Every closed substrip has , hence uniformly bounded horizontal and norms. Near either edge it has local bound , since . U013, Theorem3.1 and Corollary3.2, with , shifted to either edge and with its lower-side version, supplies both local traces and uniform compact bounds. For the bound is uniform all the way to either edge. Splitting a Schwartz test into a compact piece near zero and its complement therefore gives actual convergence in , and finite Schwartz seminorm bounds, for both traces.

Let and . Lemma L, followed by reflection and the inverse factor, gives on every interior slice. This identity also follows directly from ; its solution is justified on compact frequency tests exactly as in (L4). Here is a bounded continuous function because . Fourier continuity on , and then restriction to compact frequency tests, give and . Condition (C1) consequently forces

The smooth strictly positive multiplier never vanishes; on compact frequency sets it can be divided. Thus , first as a distribution and then pointwise by continuity. Fourier injectivity proves uniqueness of the real slice. The difference of two candidates has every real derivative zero at a real point; holomorphy makes these its complex Taylor derivatives. U015, Section3, gives the complete Cauchy/Taylor construction and hence an open zero set, and its Lemma 3.1 gives uniqueness throughout the connected strip.

For existence take the first expression in (C2). The identity shows it is holomorphic inside the strip. It decays uniformly exponentially for large . At the two boundary zeros , the numerator cancels the simple zero; the resulting quotient extends continuously on the remaining compact closed strip. Hence the required product is bounded.

Its residues at and are respectively and , by differentiating . Locally subtract these actual simple poles. The remainders extend smoothly across the relevant edge, so their traces are ordinary functions there. The singular sum is

by U013, Theorem4.1, with both signs retained. Away from zero the two traces are and its negative. The sum of the regular remainders is therefore zero off zero and, by continuity near zero, zero also at zero. Thus (C1) holds. Equation (C3), already justified for every eligible function, now gives its whole Fourier transform in (C2). No unproved contour evaluation of the hyperbolic secant is needed.
